statement: Consistent hashing is, quote unquote, the most famous algorithm of all time, and there are tons of misconceptions around it that need sorting out one by one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the most famous algorithm of all time, consistent hashing comes in. There are tons of misconceptions around it.

statement: In hash based routing the router applies a simple hash function to every incoming key; the result tells it which node to forward the request to.
detail: Contrasted with the range based approach used earlier, where ranges are held in a table at the proxy and the cache client talks to the proxy, which forwards the request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you write a simple hash function on your router side. Whenever the key comes in, hash function is applied on that key.
flags: asr: [?hash based routing | asr: "hash based out"]

statement: Routing a key to a node is how ownership of a key is defined; ownership of a key is the key concept.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is how you are defining ownership of a particular key. This is the key concept, ownership of a key.

statement: In range based routing ownership comes from key ranges (keys A to J owned by cache 1, the next range by cache 2, U to Z by cache 3); in hash based routing the hash of the key picks the owner node.
detail: The teacher said the second range as "A to T" owned by cache 2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In a hash based strategy, I would have taken hash of the key that I am passing. And it would have spit out anyone.
flags: check: teacher says "A to T are owned by cache 2" for the middle range

statement: Hash based routing is by far the most common strategy because a hash function distributes load almost uniformly across nodes: not random, but uniform enough, and deterministic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So hash based routing is by far the most common because it almost uniformly distributes the load across all things

statement: Six keys K1 to K6 on two caches (cache 0, cache 1) via the hash function: K1, K2, K6 go to cache 0 and K3, K4, K5 to cache 1, a near-equal 3:3 distribution.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So I have three is to three distribution of all my six keys. So near equal distribution, really happy.

statement: With hash based routing, adding a cache node changes the hash function from mod 2 to mod 3, so data must move: you have to go through every single key in the system and recompute where it goes.
detail: The teacher calls it a hypothetical example that shows how cruel this can get with dynamic scaling up and down. The new hash output is still deterministic (the teacher said it spits out a value in 0 to 3).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: My hash function now changes from hash function mod 2, instead of that it becomes mod 3. Now I have to do data movement

statement: After going from 2 to 3 caches: K1 stays on cache 0, K3 and K4 stay on cache 1, but K2 moves from cache 0 to cache 2, K5 from cache 1 to cache 0, and K6 from cache 0 to cache 2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So I have to take key K2, copy it from cache zero and move it to cache two.

statement: In the example the distribution stays equal, but adding one node forces moving three of the six keys (50% of the data) between nodes; this data movement is the pain point of plain hash based routing.
detail: Teacher: "So I'm doing 50% data. This is a pain point."
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm still having equal distribution, but it is requiring me to move three keys from two different nodes to three different nodes over here.

statement: Consistent hashing is not a service or a microservice, and it is not a magical solution that solves all your problems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First of all, consistent hashing is not a service, it's not a microservice, quote unquote.

statement: Next week the course covers a case where consistent hashing performs very badly and should never be used; another technique works best there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Next week we'll talk about a place where consistent hashing sucks big time.

statement: Consistent hashing solves for ownership and nothing else: it helps you determine who owns what.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Consistent hashing solves for ownership, that is it. Consistent hashing helps you determine who owns what, done and dusted, that's all it does.

statement: Consistent hashing does not do data movement or data migration for you, and it gives no uptime guarantees.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It does not do data movement for you, it does not do uptime guarantees for you.

statement: Consistent hashing is a simple technique, not really a data structure: implemented as a simple array with binary search, it takes very little space.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a simple array with binary search, that is it. It does not take a huge amount of space.

statement: The teacher has a detailed blog with Python source code on implementing your own consistent hashing, on his website under blogs (arpitbhayani.me slash consistent hashing, or Google "Arpit Bhayani consistent hashing"); he thinks it is also in the pre-reads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have a very detailed blog with Python source code on how to implement your own consistent hashing with very nice example.

statement: Consistent hashing is usually drawn as a ring; that is the simplest visual representation, but the implementation is different (read the blog for it).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: everyone just draw this ring and that's the simplest way to do it. But implementation, read that part.

statement: The things that own data (here the cache nodes) are placed on the ring by passing each node's identifier through the hash function; the output is the node's position on the ring.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the things that will own something, in this case, cache nodes, the servers are placed on consistent hashing on this ring.

statement: The ring is the hash output range 0 to 2^n: the example uses 2^4 = 16 unique values; in reality it is as large as 2^128.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In reality it is 2 raised to 128 also, so gigantic value, right?

statement: Ring example: cache 1 hashes to 3, cache 2 to 12, cache 3 to 5 and cache 4 to 10, and each node sits at that position on the ring.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you pass the identifier of cache 1 through the hash function, it spits out, let's say, 3

statement: The consistent hashing ring is implemented at whichever layer holds the routing: the client if the client routes, the proxy if a proxy routes, or the DNS-like routing component.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now where is this implemented? At your router layer.

statement: The ring is just routing information: for four nodes you store an array of four elements, no linked list or anything else; it is a very simple implementation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: All it needs to do is just have an array of four elements where you're storing this. That's it.

statement: Consistent hashing effectively replaces the routing table (the mapping of who owns which key that the router or client uses to forward requests) with a more elegant mapping; it is not a service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's just replacing this mapping in a very elegant way.

statement: To find a key's owner, the router hashes the key and picks the first node to the immediate right of that position on the ring; that node owns the key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would pick the first node to the immediate right of it to place the key there.

statement: Key K1 hashes to 0; the first node to the right of 0 is at 3, which is cache 1, so K1 is owned by cache 1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The first node to the right of 0, which is 3, 3, cache 1, so then my data goes to cache 1.

statement: With plain hash based routing, adding a node means a lot of data must be rebalanced over the network, which is very slow; consistent hashing aims to make this faster.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A lot of data movement needs to happen over network, which is very slow. So can we make it faster?

statement: Scaling from four to five nodes: cache 5 hashes to 1 and sits there on the ring, so key K1, previously owned by cache 1, is now owned by cache 5.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: key K1 that used to go to cache 1 is now owned by cache 5, because the ownership has changed.
flags: check: words possibly lost at segment boundary

statement: When a node is added, only the keys in the range now covered by the new node move (from cache 1 to cache 5); keys outside it keep going to cache 1 and all other keys are unaffected: minimal data transfer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These keys that used to go to cache one will still continue to go to cache one. All other keys remain unaffected. Minimal data transfer.

statement: Only the nodes right before and after the position where a new node is placed are affected; no other node is touched.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: only the nodes where a new node is placed, only the nodes before and after that are affected. No one else is affected.

statement: The benefit of consistent hashing is that it ensures you do only minimal data transfer when you scale up or scale down.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all it does is it ensures that you have to do minimal data transfer and you scale up or scale down.

statement: Removing a cache server (e.g. scaling down an over-provisioned cluster to save cost) has two cases: graceful termination and abrupt removal.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if I'm removing a cache server? Let's say cache one, and there are two cases.

statement: When cache 1 is removed from the ring, key K1, which used to go to cache 1, is now owned by cache 3 (the next node).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key K1 that used to go to cache one now goes to cache three

statement: Graceful removal: take a snapshot of cache 1, copy its data to cache 3, and only then remove cache 1 from the ring, so requests landing on cache 3 do not cause cache misses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You'll take the data from cache one, copy it to cache three and then remove it from the ring
flags: check: words possibly lost at segment boundary

statement: Abrupt removal (the server goes down): all the load for the range that went to cache 1 suddenly goes to cache 3, and you should be okay with that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all the load for this range that used to go to cache one will now suddenly go to cache three.

statement: In removal too, all other keys remain unaffected, so the data transfer is minimal.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because all other keys, all other other keys, they remain unaffected. Again, minimal data transfer.

statement: The teacher has used consistent hashing in production, which is why he is confident about what it does and does not do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've used consistent hashing in production, that's what I'm so confident about it, that what it does and what it does not.

statement: Stay away from the many consistent hashing misconceptions on the internet; understand the one problem it solves and how it solves it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: so try to stay away from them and understand what one problem does it solve and how it solves it.

statement: If you add a blank new cache server to the ring, the keys it now owns are not there, causing cache misses and higher load on the backend systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would lead to cache miss. So higher load on the backend systems that you have.

statement: Operationally, to add cache 5: take a snapshot of cache 1, prepare cache 5 from it, add cache 5 to the ring so requests for K1 find the data, then slowly delete the keys that moved.
detail: The transcript says to delete the data from cache five / take the snapshot of cache five at 02:22:35; the Q&A at 02:50:52 says the snapshot is of cache 1 and the data is deleted on cache 1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You take the snapshot of cache one, you add cache five and then add it to this ring.
flags: check: which cache the snapshot is taken of and keys deleted from (said "cache five")

statement: A lot of people use consistent hashing because it gives you just one thing, minimal data transfer; there is no magic sauce behind it; it is very simple and beautiful in hindsight.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's why a lot of people use consistent hashing, because it gives you just one thing. Minimal data transfer.

statement: The distributed cache designed in class is nothing but a distributed hash table (DHT).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What we just designed, a distributed cache, is actually nothing but a distributed hash table.

statement: The entire internet, the BitTorrent network and the Bitcoin network are distributed hash tables.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The entire internet is a distributed hash table. The BitTorrent network is a distributed hash table.
flags: check: possible ASR duplicate of the BitTorrent line

statement: A DHT is a generic concept: store the underlying data in memory and it becomes a distributed cache, on storage and it becomes distributed storage; only the applications built on top change.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just change the underlying storage and store it in memory. It becomes distributed cache.

statement: The idea of a distributed hash table is that there is no central entity everyone talks to; a distributed cache can likewise choose not to use a central routing server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Idea of a distributed hash table is that there is no central entity that everyone talks to.

statement: At internet scale (e.g. BitTorrent) you talk to the nearest server: if it has the data it responds, otherwise it forwards the request or returns the IP address of another machine to go to; the lookup always converges.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It always converges back and that's the property of it.

statement: Adding or removing a node in a DHT must cause minimal data movement (even when a server goes down and another takes its place), which is why consistent-hashing-like techniques are used to implement any DHT.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which is why consistent hashing like algorithms or techniques are used in implementation of any distributed hash table

statement: A system with no central entity that must do minimal data transfer when nodes go up and down falls into the category of DHTs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you need to do minimal data transfer when your node goes up and down, that falls into the category of DHTs

statement: DHTs are everywhere: distributed file systems (the teacher calls our distributed cache an example of one), DNS servers, instant messaging / IRC clients, P2P networks like BitTorrent, and IPFS.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DNS servers are DHTs. Instant messaging app, IRC clients, you might have heard of those, were DHTs.

statement: IPFS (InterPlanetary File System, ipfs.io) is a distributed file system/DHT where people store data such as blockchain and NFT data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you have not heard of it, look for IPFS.io.

statement: Optional: the teacher has a 45-minute deep-dive video on the Kademlia paper in his YouTube BitTorrent series; it took him three days to understand and he calls it a mind-blowing implementation the world uses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have 45 minutes of deep dive into this paper called Kademlia, mind-blowing implementation.

statement: Kademlia solves DHT routing: no node knows about every other node, yet the request still gets routed and converges to the node that has the data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, but then still it tends to somehow route the request and converge it to the node that has it.

statement: High availability, for a cache as for persistent storage in basic concept, is achieved by adding replicas: every node has a replica that takes its place if the node goes down, at the cost of maintaining the extra node.
detail: Teacher: if availability is important for you, you do that; for persistent storage things might be a little different.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If a node goes down, replica takes its place, but it comes with its cost of maintaining that other node

statement: Alternatively, keep copies of a node's data on other nodes of the ring (cache 1's data also on cache 3, cache 3's on cache 4), so if cache 3 goes down cache 4 can serve its requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say whatever data is on cache 1, I have one copy of it in cache 3.

statement: The ring lets you set a replication factor: with replication factor 2 (as stated) the node that owns a key stores it and the two nodes immediately after it on the ring also hold the data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which means the node that owns it stores it and two nodes immediately after that in the ring would have the data.

statement: Data redundancy, across nodes or via a standby server/replica, is the way to get high availability: if a node goes down you know where to find its data and can reconstruct it; it is standard practice for reliability and important even for a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So data redundancy is a way to get high availability, either across nodes or across system.

statement: Redis has the AOF (append only file), Redis's write-ahead log: every write is appended to the file, and when the cache rebuilds (e.g. after a reboot) Redis loads everything from it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So even Redis has this AOF file format, which is Redis's write-ahead log. It's called AOF, append only file.

statement: An append only file is the standard way to ensure durability (the teacher first said reliability, then corrected himself: durability is the right word).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Standard way to ensure reliability or durability. Actually, durability is the right one.

statement: Recap of making a cache distributed - storage: store data on separate nodes with logic to determine ownership; hash based and range based routing are the two very common ways.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: with some logic to determine ownership, hash based routing, partition, range based routing, two very common ways to do it.

statement: There are four ways to do routing and they apply to any distributed system; not every one suits every case, each has pros and cons, so pick your battles.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, when it comes to routing, there are four ways to do routing. It applies to any distributed system in the world.

statement: This concludes the distributed cache: a lot of time on single-node implementation, then routing in depth, availability with replicas, and scaling with consistent hashing (minimal data transfer when adding nodes).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And this concludes everything about distributed cache.

statement: Redis's DNS-like routing (redirecting the client) avoids putting a load balancer in front, to keep the infrastructure simple: let the node itself take care of it.
detail: Student 5 proposed it; the teacher answered "Exactly. Why to have another [unclear: couple], let the node itself take care of that."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: could not decide to use a load balancer. Was it to just simplify the infrastructure to use it?

statement: Redis does the redirect only for replicas: if you fire a write request on a replica, it returns the master's IP address and asks you to connect there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if you're firing a write request on replica, it's you the IP address of the master and request you to connect to that.

statement: For reads both ways exist in Redis: Redis Sentinel addresses it and Redis now also has a proxy that holds routing information; the teacher is not sure how routing works in today's Sentinel setup and suggests watching talks on it.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: Both ways are there. So Redis Sentinel solves that problem. So Redis is evolving.

statement: A real system can mix two or more of the routing approaches for different operations.
detail: Student 5's takeaway; the teacher replied "Yeah, for each of these."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So my takeaway is that it can be a mix of two or more of these approaches for different ways.

statement: Returning the master node's IP address when a write hits a read replica is the most common approach; almost all databases adopt it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That is the most common way. Almost all databases adopt this.

statement: Alternatively a database can just discard a write on a replica and return an error telling the client to find the master itself; the teacher compares the two to humans: some say "go find it on your own", others kindly tell you where to go.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Either a database can choose to just discard the request and return an error and say, go find the master node.

statement: Nodes can end up placed too close together on the ring; that is a disadvantage of consistent hashing because placement is not in your control.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Yes, then that's a disadvantage of consistent hash because it's not in your control.

statement: Consistent hashing also suffers from hot partitions (densely populated areas of the ring): you hand control to the hash function to distribute keys uniformly enough, but if the key distribution and the hash function are bad you see hotspots, one node much hotter than others, and then you add one more node just to try to mitigate it.
detail: Asked by Student 2 (whether certain areas of the ring can be densely populated); the teacher: "Yes, very much possible."
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hot partition problem. That is there. Consistent hashing suffers from both.

statement: Companies still use consistent hashing despite these problems because it makes scaling up and down simple enough, and the hash range is so long (said as 2^120) that everyone is playing by the odds.
detail: Earlier (02:14:21) the teacher gave 2^128 as the real range.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The range is not short enough, it's long enough, two raised to power 120,

statement: Virtual nodes (dividing the ring into many small virtual parts mapped to physical nodes) work against consistent hashing's goal: if one server goes down, many non-consecutive chunks have to move instead of a single neighbour transfer.
detail: Student 1's doubt; the teacher answered "Yes. A thousand times. Yes." - this is exactly the disadvantage of virtual nodes.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Then if one server goes down, I see a lot of chunks has to move, in place of the current strategy that you have.

statement: In a stateful system like this cache, adding cache 5 was operationally simple: take a quick snapshot of cache 1 and load the new node from it; an efficient, nothing-fancy data movement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We took the snapshot of cache 1 and put it over here. It made life so simple for us.

statement: With virtual nodes a new node is placed at multiple places on the ring, so its data must be loaded from multiple other nodes: operationally challenging, you might miss something, and one slow source node slows the whole process.
detail: The teacher notes that whenever someone explains consistent hashing they talk about virtual nodes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this node will be placed at multiple places. Now from multiple other places, you have to load data on this server. Operationally that becomes challenging.

statement: Adding virtual nodes is not a good idea to solve the hot partition problem in a stateful use case; companies still do it and there are hacks around it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So adding virtual nodes is not a good idea to solve hot partition problem. And it is stateful use case, not a good idea.

statement: Virtual nodes bring back a lot of network transfer, copying from many places instead of one, which is exactly what consistent hashing was adopted to reduce.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They're doing, still doing a lot of network transfer, which you started consistent hashing just to reduce that.

statement: Virtual nodes are not the worst, just bad enough: fine if you are operationally okay with the network transfer; the teacher prefers keeping things operationally simple (copy one node, bring the server up, done) because simple systems scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So I would like to keep things simple as compared to things operationally complex, because simple systems scale.

statement: The single-node implementation shown in class (including the malloc implementation) works because the cache is single threaded; making it concurrent would cause massive havoc, and single threading also saves context-switch costs.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: If it, you put a concurrent thing, it would be a havoc, right?
flags: check: speaker - "Yes, massive, massive havoc" may be the Teacher

statement: Single threading oversimplifies a lot of things without losing concurrency, but under-utilises the hardware; you can put multiple Redis nodes on one machine to use it, so there are trade-offs everywhere.
detail: Student 2 agreed it is a better idea than introducing the complexity of concurrency for this use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So basically single threaded makes a lot of things oversimplified

statement: Memory use beyond limits is controlled in practice by kernel-level ulimits per process and by limits configurable in the malloc library itself (GNU malloc, tcmalloc, jemalloc), so one service cannot push a shared node to 98-99%; generally people don't use GNU malloc.
detail: Student 2: what the teacher described happens with kmalloc - without limits, every write page-faults and allocates a page until physical memory is exhausted. The teacher: "Super... my understanding is correct."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: one is kernel level U limits, like each process. When you set U limits, two is with the malloc library limits itself.

statement: When you exceed those limits you generally get a SIGABRT and the program does crash: the kernel kills the process to save itself.
detail: Student 2's explanation, endorsed by the teacher.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the program does crash, right? Where you hit the program will crash because kernel will kill you the moment you exceed those limits.

statement: SIGABRT cannot really be handled: it signals that the instruction pipeline is done; you can run some last code but the process is killed. The teacher: program does crash, you can't handle much; he will refine the course material for the next quarter.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: it is a signal where you are saying your instruction pipeline is done.

statement: When a transaction holding a shared lock updates the row, the lock is elevated to an exclusive lock.
detail: Student 6 implemented shared locks for the week-2 seat allocation exercise (120 seats, 120 people) and saw the same seats given to many people.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you update, the lock elevates to your exclusive lock and then it doesn't update.

statement: Several people getting the same seat with shared locks should not happen; the first thing to check is the isolation level.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That should not have happened. What was your isolation level?

statement: To debug locking, use the MySQL administrative console (not the UI) to see which row holds which lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: but you can check which row is getting which lock.

statement: Repeatable read is almost the most common isolation level out there; the teacher assumes it for his explanation, stating it is his guess and he might be wrong.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm assuming the isolation level is repeatable read, which is the most common one out there, almost.

statement: Teacher's guess at the bug, reduced to two transactions on one row: both take a shared lock; T2 writes first, so its lock is elevated to exclusive; T1 still holds its shared lock, waits until the exclusive lock is released, then writes to the same row, overwriting it.
detail: Teacher said the explanation was clear in his head and he restated it more simply; he swaps T1/T2 mid-explanation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When it is trying to write it, it waits until an existing exclusive lock is released. Once it released, it wrote to the same location.

statement: The overwrite happens because the waiting transaction does not re-evaluate its statement after the lock is released.
detail: Student 6 confirmed it was overwriting; the teacher said "this is most probably what is happening behind the scene".
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, which means that it is not revaluating the statement.

statement: Use Percona, a MySQL plugin/utility, to visualise and manage locking state of databases (it has a lock viewer, name not recalled); the teacher used it in 2015.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is a tool called Percona, which you can use to visualize this as well.

statement: The odd behaviour could also be a bug; deadlock data is very hard to interpret, which is the gap between practical understanding and production, where things go berserk and nobody knows what is happening.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when things hit production, things go berserk and we have no idea what's happening.

statement: A deadlock does not crash the database or the program; it terminates the transaction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Deadlock does not lead to database crash. Deadlock leads to termination of transaction.

statement: Connection pooling is not a property of the programming language (the teacher first says it is a property of the database, then that it is really a property of the application logic or library you write).
detail: Student 6 said the teacher had claimed PHP doesn't support connection pooling; the teacher said he never said that and has not worked deeply on PHP.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: connection pooling is property of database, not of language.
flags: check: 03:03:58-03:04:03 may be a student interjection

statement: A connection pool is just multiple TCP connections established with the database plus a queue to manage them; you may find a library that manages the pool for you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: establishing multiple TCP connections with the database and having a queue to manage it. That's it. That's what a connection pool is.

statement: You can write your own connection pool in a day; all you need is a blocking queue.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can just spend a day, write your own connection pool. It's that simple.

statement: The only requirement for building a connection pool is that the database keeps a connection open and does not terminate it unless you ask it to.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your database should not terminate the connection unless you ask it to terminate.

statement: One CDC can push to multiple sinks such as Elasticsearch and Redshift; the diagram drew separate CDCs only for visual clarity.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: But if you'd want to just fan out to multiple things, you can do that.

statement: A CDC fanning out to several sinks has high memory utilisation because it performs a different transformation per sink (JSON for Elasticsearch, another format for MySQL, something else for a third sink), so CDCs need to scale up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So CDCs would need to scale up of it. That's it. It would have high memory utilization.
